summary: Maurice Jametel (1856–1889) was a scholar of Sinology and Tibetology. He studied at the École nationale des langues orientales vivantes, where he later held an academic post around 1886 to 1889 and taught Édouard Chavannes.
Maurice Lehot (d. 1931) was an Indologist. He studied at the University of Lyon under Félix Lacôte and served as a schoolteacher (professor) at the Lycée d'Aix-en-Provence.

Maurice Leroy (1909–1990) was a linguist who earned his doctorate at the Université libre de Bruxelles and studied under Theodor Bloch, Joseph Vendryes, and Émile Benveniste at the EPHE. He served as professor at Brussels and Secrétaire perpétuel of the Royal Academy of Belgium.

Maurice O'Connell Walshe (1911–1998) was a linguist and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at UCL, Berlin, Göttingen, Vienna, and with Walpola Rahula. He taught German at Leeds, UCL, Nottingham, and Bedford College, and was Deputy Director at the University of London.

Maurice Phillips (1839–1910) was a scholar of Indology and religious studies. Educated at Bedford College and the University of Bern (Ph.D.), he served as a missionary with the London Missionary Society (1862–1908) and was a Fellow at the University of Madras.
Maurice Wiles (1923–2005) was a scholar in religious studies. He was educated at Tonbridge School and Christ's College, Cambridge, and taught Michael Pye.
Maurice Wilmotte (1861–1942) was a Belgian scholar in linguistics. He studied at the University of Liège from 1881 to 1885 and later held a post there from around 1895 until 1931.

Maurine Stuart (1922–1990) was a Buddhist studies practitioner. She studied at the University of Manitoba and under Nadia Boulanger, Hakuun Ryoko Yasutani, Eido Shimano, and Soen Nakagawa, later serving as president and spiritual director of the Cambridge Buddhist Association from 1979.

Maurizio Taddei (1936–2000) was a scholar of archaeology, Indology, and Central Asian studies. He studied at Sapienza under Mario Bussagli and held posts at the Museo Nazionale d'Arte Orientale, University of Naples "L'Orientale", and the Italian Institute for Africa and the East.

Mauro Maggi is a scholar of Central Asian studies, Buddhist studies, and linguistics. He studied at Naples "L'Orientale" and under Ronald Eric Emmerick, later holding posts at Sapienza University of Rome and the Italian Institute for Africa and the East as Director.

Mavis L. Fenn is a religious and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the Universities of Winnipeg, Calgary, and McMaster under Graeme MacQueen. She held posts at St. Paul's University College and the University of Waterloo, where she chaired Religious Studies.

Max Arthur Macauliffe (1841–1913) was a scholar of religious studies and Indology. He completed his education at Springfield College and the University of Galway, earning a B.A. between 1857 and 1863.

Max Deeg is an Indologist, Buddhist studies, and Sinology scholar who completed his Habilitation at Würzburg. He has held positions at Nagoya University, the University of Vienna, Cardiff University as Head of School, and the International Institute for Buddhist Studies.

Max Hunter Harrison (1893–1986) was a scholar of religion and Indology. Educated at Knox, Andover Newton, Harvard, and Columbia, he taught at Jaffna College, served as Principal of United Theological College, Bangalore (1931–1958), and was acting director at the Missionary Research Library.

Max Jakob Niedermann (1874–1954) was a linguist who studied at Zurich, Basel, and under Wackernagel, Thurneysen, Meillet, and Havet. He served as professor at the University of Neuchâtel and ord. Professor of comparative linguistics and Sanskrit at the University of Basel.

Max Kaltenmark (1910–2002) was a scholar of Sinology and religious studies who succeeded Henri Maspero. He led the Centre Franco-Chinois d'Études Sinologiques, directed the EFEO (1949–1953), and held posts at the EPHE and the University of Paris.

Max Leopold Margolis (1866–1932) was a linguist and religious studies scholar who earned his Ph.D. at Columbia. He held posts at Columbia, Hebrew Union College, UC Berkeley, and occupied the chair of biblical philology at Dropsie College from 1909 to 1932.

Max Lindenau was an Indologist who studied at the Universities of Munich, Greifswald, and Leipzig, where he earned his doctorate under Ernst Windisch. He later served as Privatdozent at the University of Marburg from 1919 to 1927.

Max Oidtmann (b. 1979) is a historian, Sinologist, and Tibetologist educated at Carleton College, Indiana University, and Harvard under Mark Elliott. He served as Assistant Professor at Georgetown University in Qatar and became a professor at the University of Munich in 2021.

Max Scheler (1874–1928) was a philosopher who studied at the universities of Munich, Berlin, and Jena. Over his career, he taught Edward Conze and held academic appointments at the universities of Jena, Munich, Göttingen, and Cologne.
